papers.title: Selective Bacteroidota Depletion but Not Global Microbiome Differences in Short Bowel Syndrome on Fiber-Free Enteral Nutrition
papers.abstract: Intestinal dysbiosis in pediatric short bowel syndrome (SBS) is associated with poor growth, but the factors that are driving this dysbiosis remain unclear. Prior studies suggest that parenteral nutrition (PN) dependence and remnant intestinal anatomy are correlated with dysbiosis. However, these studies often compared SBS patients to healthy controls, making it difficult to distinguish SBS-specific factors from alterations due to differences in diet, namely the consumption of enteral nutrition with complex composition and exposure to dietary fiber. In this preliminary report from the GREENBEANS study, we examined baseline stool shotgun metagenomic profiles from 10 SBS patients and 13 non-SBS controls receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition. Alpha diversity did not differ significantly between groups by richness or Shannon diversity. Beta diversity showed minimal separation by Bray-Curtis distance and modest separation in Jaccard distance. Differential abundance analysis identified depletion of Bacteroidota in SBS. Compared to control patients also receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition, SBS was associated with only a small global difference in the gut microbiome, suggesting that diet, and not anatomy as previously assumed, is the predominant determinant of gut microbiome structure. This suggests that the inclusion of complex substrates, such as dietary fiber, in enteral nutrition, may be a modality to prevent the development of a dysbiotic microbiome in patients with SBS.

papers.title: Interval colorectal cancer risk by haemoglobin concentration in Australia's National Bowel Cancer Screening Program
papers.abstract: Background Interval colorectal cancers (CRCs) are an important measure of screening performance. We assessed interval CRC risk after negative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT), its association with faecal haemoglobin (f-Hb) concentration, and differences by age and sex in Australia s National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP). Methods We conducted a population-based retrospective cohort study linking Queensland screening and cancer registry records for NBCSP participants aged 50-74 years screened in 2018-2022. Eligible episodes had f-Hb below 20 ug/g in both samples. We excluded episodes with CRC diagnosed on or before follow-up start. Follow-up ended at CRC, the next screening episode, death, 24 months, or December 31, 2023. We estimated adjusted cause-specific hazard ratios (HRs), accounting for repeated episodes within participants, and cumulative incidence with death and subsequent screening as competing events. Findings Among 1,083,149 negative screening episodes from 700,734 participants, 586 interval CRCs occurred over 2,056,405 person-years. The incidence rate was 28.5 per 100,000 person-years, and 24-month cumulative incidence was 57.6 per 100,000 episodes (95% CI 53.1-62.5). Risk increased with age and was higher in males (adjusted HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.08-1.50). The complete-case quantitative cohort included 326,931 episodes and 138 cancers. Compared with maximum f-Hb of 0-5 ug/g, concentrations >15-<20 ug/g were associated with an adjusted HR of 14.93 (9.02-24.70). Corresponding 24-month risks were 35.7 (28.5-44.7) and 504.5 (323.4-787.0) per 100,000 episodes. Higher negative-range f-Hb concentrations were more common in older participants and males. The quantitative cohort showed no clear sex difference after adjustment for f-Hb. Interpretation CRC risk varies substantially among people with a negative screening result. Quantitative F-Hb levels may help identify who is at higher risk of interval CRC. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and assess the benefits, harms and costs of changing screening intervals.

papers.title: Detection of Human Bocavirus in Stool Samples Collected During an Outbreak of Acute Gastroenteritis in Children in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil
papers.abstract: Introduction: This study investigated human bocavirus (HBoV) in samples obtained during an outbreak of acute gastroenteritis (AGE) among children in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. AGE is characterized by symptoms including diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fever and may require hospitalization in severe cases. Methods: A total of 131 stool samples collected from children hospitalized with AGE at a hospital in Salvador, Bahia, were analyzed. HBoV was detected using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested PCR). Positive samples were sequenced and inoculated into Vero cell cultures, followed by sodium dodecyl sulfate- polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and Western blotting. Results: Of the 131 samples analyzed, 13 tested positive for HBoV. Children aged 0-4 years were the most affected by AGE and showed the highest frequency of HBoV detection. HBoV was successfully cultured in Vero cells, representing a novel finding reported in this study. Subsequent SDS-PAGE and Western blot analyses revealed protein bands suggestive of HBoV structural proteins. Conclusion: This study highlights the need for accurate diagnostic methods and preventive strategies to control the spread of HBoV and other pathogens associated with gastroenteritis in pediatric populations.

papers.title: IBDex: A Frozen Patient-Scale Atlas for Bulk Transcriptomics in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Background & AimsBulk mucosal RNA sequencing in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is analyzed one cohort at a time, so each study rebuilds its own molecular scale. We aimed to build a frozen atlas that new cohorts could use without retraining. MethodsWe built IBDex from 3,168 intestinal biopsies from 1,680 patients with Crohns disease, ulcerative colitis or no IBD, drawn from four cohorts. Patients were kept within a single training, validation or test partition. A tissue-aware conditional variational autoencoder with adversarial suppression of cohort identity was trained on a 3,000-gene interface. The scaling, encoder, decoder, pathway basis and phenotype directions were then frozen. Phenotype-anchored counterfactual perturbation (PACP) produced anatomy-conditioned gene-response maps. We tested the atlas without parameter updates in three unseen IBD cohorts, a longitudinal olamkicept trial, and cohorts with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) or colorectal cancer (CRC). ResultsIn held-out data, dataset identity fell to near chance (balanced accuracy 0.307 vs 0.250). Anatomy, diagnosis and inflammation remained recoverable (inflammation AUC 0.82). Marginal differential expression conflated inflammation and disease state ({rho} = 0.834). PACP separated them ({rho} = -0.161), with inflammation driven by TNF-NF-{kappa}B, and disease state by proliferative, type I interferon and metabolic programs. In 93 patients in combined endoscopic and histological remission, inflammation approached controls (AUC 0.58), but disease state stayed displaced (AUC 0.725, P = 1.8 x 10{square}1{square}). The frozen atlas recovered clinical, single-cell-defined and disease-behavior structure in unseen cohorts. It also tracked responder trajectories during olamkicept therapy and separated PSC (patient-level AUC 0.794) and CRC (AUC 0.938- 1.000). Where de novo differential expression became unreliable, transferred response maps stayed reproducible ({rho} [≥] 0.89). ConclusionsIBDex turns historical bulk biopsy data into a reusable reference. It shows that deep remission moves inflammation toward control levels but leaves a persistent molecular disease state.

papers.title: Understanding Psychological Health in Adults with Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: BackgroundPsychological health is an important aspect of health and well-being among adults with irritable bowel syndrome, yet the interrelationships among individual vulnerabilities, social experiences, perceived stress, and psychological health outcomes remain poorly understood. ObjectiveTo characterize psychological health and examine direct and indirect associations of childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms within an adapted Stress Process Model. DesignCross-sectional secondary analysis. SettingThe United States All of Us Research Program. Participants2,417 adults with electronic health record-documented irritable bowel syndrome and complete data on the primary analysis variables and covariates. MethodsSeparate structural equation models examined childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms in relation to perceived stress, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and positive psychological well-being, with loneliness and perceived social support as psychosocial pathways. Models adjusted for sociodemographic and social-context factors. ResultsThe median age was 54.39 years; 80.7% were female and 84.4% were White. Moderate-to-high perceived stress was reported by 56.2%, at least moderate anxiety symptoms by 21.0%, and at least moderate depressive symptoms by 24.3%. Higher ACE-8 scores were associated with greater perceived stress, anxiety symptoms, and depressive symptoms and lower psychological well-being ({beta} = 0.063, 0.089, 0.116, and -0.100, respectively); corresponding associations for higher ASRS-6 scores were {beta} = 0.299, 0.355, 0.390, and -0.260. Loneliness-specific indirect associations were positive for perceived stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (ACE-8: {beta} = 0.023-0.034; ASRS-6: {beta} = 0.043-0.075) and negative for psychological well-being (ACE-8: {beta} = -0.039; ASRS-6: {beta} = -0.089; all p < .001). Social support-specific indirect associations were not significant in the ACE-8 model and were small and significant only for anxiety and depression in the ASRS-6 model ({beta} = 0.003-0.004). ConclusionsPsychological health among adults with irritable bowel syndrome was associated with interconnected individual and social factors within an adapted Stress Process Model. Childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms showed direct and indirect associations with psychological health, with loneliness emerging as the most consistent social factor. These findings support prospective investigation of individual vulnerabilities and social experiences in psychological health. The cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation. What is already knownO_LIPsychological distress is common in adults with irritable bowel syndrome. C_LIO_LILoneliness and perceived social support describe distinct social experiences. C_LI What this paper addsO_LIChildhood adversity and adult attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity symptom burden were linked to psychological health. C_LIO_LILoneliness was associated with distress and lower psychological well-being. C_LI

papers.title: Detection and Characterization of Human Bocavirus in Stool Samples from an Acute Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, in 2024.
papers.abstract: IntroductionAcute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a global public health problem and a major cause of mortality in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Human bocavirus (HBoV) is among the viral agents associated with this condition. Therefore, investigating the presence of HBoV in cases of AGE in Salvador, Bahia, as well as its prevalence and circulating strains, is important. ObjectiveTo investigate the occurrence of HBoV infection during an AGE outbreak in Salvador. MethodsA total of 178 samples were analyzed for HBoV using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested PCR), and the amplification products were visualized by agarose gel electrophoresis. HBoV was detected in 5.7% of the samples analyzed. ConclusionThis study contributes to the understanding of HBoV epidemiology as a secondary agent associated with acute gastroenteritis during a norovirus outbreak in Salvador. Continued investigation and identification of the etiological agents involved in outbreaks are essential for evaluating the causes of AGE. These findings also highlight the need for broader diagnostic approaches and the importance of phylogenetic analysis for monitoring and controlling viral infections.

papers.title: Adenovirus as a Causative Agent of an Acute Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil.
papers.abstract: IntroductionAcute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a cause of childhood morbidity and may be associated with human adenovirus (HAdV) infection. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence of HAdV in fecal samples from children with AGE in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, as well as to molecularly characterize the identified strains and evaluate their cytopathic effects in cell culture. MethodsA total of 131 samples were analyzed using the nested polymerase chain reaction (Nested-PCR) technique. Molecular characterization was performed through Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, while Vero cell cultures were used to investigate the occurrence of cytopathic effects. ResultsOf the samples analyzed, 13 (9.9%) tested positive for HAdV, while 118 (90.1%) were negative. The highest detection frequency was observed in children aged three years or younger, particularly those under one year of age. Phylogenetic analysis identified variants related to HAdV-F41 and HAdV-B3, revealing genetic differences and distinct clustering patterns compared with reference sequences. In cell culture, cytopathic effects were observed four days after inoculation, although further analyses are required to confirm productive viral replication. ConclusionThese findings demonstrate the presence of HAdV in the samples studied and contribute to understanding its genetic diversity and circulation in Salvador, highlighting the importance of epidemiological surveillance and further studies on its role in the etiology of childhood AGE.

papers.title: Protracted copy number alteration evolution in Barrett's oesophagus leading to oesophageal cancer
papers.abstract: Detection of copy number alterations (CNAs) in Barretts oesophagus (BO) predicts oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) risk. When CNAs first occur is unknown. Here we show that CNAs typically form in BO many decades prior to first clinical detection of BO or cancer, and often during childhood. Using a novel molecular clock analysis, we analysed spatiotemporal longitudinal whole genome data from 80 individuals within BO surveillance. Chr 9p loss of heterozygosity (LOH) tended to be the first CNA event typically occurring at age 10-30 years. Genome doubling (GD) also typically originated multiple decades prior to cancer develop. Patients who progressed to OAC had an enrichment of CNAs late in life. CNA rate was more predictive of cancer risk than CNA burden. Analysis of OAC whole genomes confirmed the early-life origins of cancer-associated CNAs. The malignant transformation potential of BO may be set during the first decades of life, enabling early cancer interception.

papers.title: Sedatives reduce human gastric slow-wave amplitude, assessed by a multicenter study of endoscopic gastric mapping
papers.abstract: BackgroundGastrointestinal (GI) motility disorders are prevalent, impose a significant burden, and are associated with disrupted spatial propagation of bioelectrical gastric slow waves. High-resolution endoscopic gastric mapping (EGM) is an emerging minimally invasive technique for imaging gastric electrical activity; however, EGM is performed alongside standard gastroscopy and requires procedural sedation, which may interact with gastric electrical activity, distorting clinical insights. This study explored the influence of procedural sedation on EGM-recorded slow-wave activity. MethodsEGM was performed for [~]7 min in 32 patients undergoing upper GI endoscopy at two New Zealand hospitals. Endoscopists administered procedural sedation (fentanyl and midazolam) according to best clinical practice. The relationship between slow-wave amplitude and patient characteristics was then investigated using a variety of statistical techniques. Key ResultsGastric slow waves were detected in 30 of 32 patients who underwent EGM. Symptom scores and demographic measures were comparable between sites. Fentanyl (A, 93.4 {+/-} 13.7 g vs B, 137.5 {+/-} 33.7 g, p[≤]0.001) and midazolam (A, 5.0 {+/-} 0.9 mg vs B, 7.4 {+/-} 1.6 mg, p[≤]0.001) doses were higher at Hospital B than Hospital A. Correspondingly, slow-wave amplitudes were lower at Hospital B than Hospital A (A, 2.33 {+/-} 1.61 mV vs B, 0.86 {+/-} 1.01 mV, p=0.004). All other slow-wave metrics were consistent between hospitals. Combined sedative dose was negatively correlated with slow-wave amplitude (p=0.037). Conclusions & InferencesHigher procedural sedative doses are associated with lower-amplitude gastric slow-waves. Procedural sedation dose and opiate administration should be carefully considered when interpreting GI electrophysiology measurements.

papers.title: Serum proteins predict incident inflammatory bowel disease 14 years before diagnosis: a machine-learning and Cox modelling in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Using an analysis pipeline that combines machine learning-based feature selection with classical statistical modelling, we aimed to predict incident inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and to identify candidate proteins associated with disease development. We used UK Biobank data in an observational cohort study of 52,331 participants with proteomics data and without a history of IBD. The cohort was split into an 80/20 train/test dataset, and three separate extreme gradient boosting models were trained on the training dataset. Using Shapley values, we ranked the predictive importance of 2,912 proteins for incident IBD, Crohns disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). The top 20 proteins per outcome served as features in multivariate Cox models predicting 350 incident cases over 14 years. All three proteomics Cox models showed moderate discrimination in the test dataset, with the UC model performing the best (C-index: 0.68), followed by IBD (C-index: 0.65), and CD (C-index: 0.60). All proteomics models outperformed clinical models. Smoking remained the only significant clinical predictor in the combined proteomics + clinical model. 48 unique proteins were identified across the three models, with 16 reaching statistical significance (p< 0.05). Machine learning-based feature selection with statistical survival modelling identifies plasma proteins that predict incident IBD and highlight biologically plausible, potentially targetable pathways in the preclinical phase of IBD.

papers.title: Replacing animal-sourced with plant-sourced proteins alters gut microbiota and biomarkers associated with colorectal cancer risk in healthy adults: A randomized feeding study
papers.abstract: Epidemiological studies associate replacing animal-sourced with plant-sourced protein with lower colorectal cancer (CRC) risk, but controlled feeding studies have rarely tested how this substitution alters the gut microbiota and CRC-related biomarkers. In a 12-week randomized controlled feeding study, 136 healthy adults consumed diets providing 30 energy percent (E%), 50 E%, or 70 E% of protein from plant sources. Change in gut microbiota composition was the primary outcome; stool characteristics, fecal N-nitroso compounds (NOCs), and fecal and plasma bile acids (BAs) were secondary outcomes. The 70% plant-protein diet significantly restructured the gut microbiota, increasing fiber-associated Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia while reducing Methanobrevibacter and several asaccharolytic taxa. Microbial functional potential shifted toward plant-carbohydrate degradation, with lower amino acid degradation and methanogenesis. Fecal pH decreased, stool characteristics suggested faster colonic transit, and potentially carcinogenic total and haem-derived NOCs declined progressively with plant-protein replacement. The 70% plant-protein diet also reduced fecal secondary and taurine-conjugated BAs, including the CRC-associated BAs DCA and LCA. Plasma glucuronidated BAs increased, expanding the circulating pool of readily excreted BA conjugates. Higher insoluble fiber intake was associated with greater microbiota restructuring and lower fecal NOCs. Methanogen carriers had higher baseline fecal NOCs and features of slower colonic transit, and showed weaker microbiota and less favorable BA responses to the 70% plant-protein diet. Baseline methanogen carriage thus could be exploited for participant stratification in future dietary interventions. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03206827.

papers.title: Disrupted microbial queuosine biosynthesis contributes to dysbiosis of human inflammatory bowel disease
papers.abstract: Background and AimsAs a microbiome/diet-derived vitamin, queuine (q) is a micronutrient that eukaryotes acquire from microbiota or diet. Vitamin q, the free base form of queuosine (Q), is used for Q-modification of transfer RNA (tRNA). Although tRNA-Q-modification in regulating eukaryotic cell physiology is recognized, the relationship between Q-tRNA-modification and the human microbiome in health and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) remains unknown. Which bacteria produce q and how the q-producing bacteria contributing to human health and IBD are not explored. Here, we hypothesize that disrupted microbial Q-biosynthesis contributes to the dysbiosis of human IBD. We performed comprehensive multi-omics integrative analyses using publicly available datasets. Specifically, we re-analyzed publicly available shotgun metagenomic, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), metabolic datasets, and completed meta-analysis. MethodsTo systematically investigate microbial Q-biosynthesis in healthy individuals and IBD patients, we performed a systematic secondary analysis by integrating 9 publicly available metagenomic datasets, 15 scRNA-seq datasets and one metabolic dataset published prior to 2026. We present a novel secondary bioinformatic reanalysis of sequence outputs mapped to the latest microbial taxonomy, functional pathways and microbial Q-related genes. Longitudinal study of shotgun metagenomics across the human lifespan (3146 samples) enabled taxonomic and functional profiling. ResultsWe first identified key q-producing bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes) in healthy populations. We then found that patients with IBD had significantly reducation of q-producing bacteria and a coordinated downregulation of the Q-related pathways, including Q, preQ0, de novo guanosine ribonucleotide biosynthesis and de novo guanosine deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis pathways. This functional impairment was primarily driven by reduced contributions from Bacteroides, Alistipes and Akkermansia. The longitudinal stability of the q-producing bacteria community across the human lifespan (1638 samples). We observed a significant negative correlation between host age and the abundance of q-producing bacteria in patients with UC. Moreover, Queuine tRNA-ribosyltransferase 1 (QTRT1) expression in human intestinal epithelial cells was significantly reduced in patients with IBD compared to healthy controls. ConclusionsOur study used multi-omics datasets to define a novel functional dysbiosis characterized by a reduction of microbial Q-biosynthesis in patients with IBD. Vitamin q and its tRNA modification is lesser-recognized in human IBD. Understanding the cellular and organismal mechanisms of this microbiome-dependent micronutrient will advance the prevention of IBD and improve the quality of life of patients with IBD. What is already known on this topic?Queuine, vitamin q, is a highly conserved hypermodified nucleoside micronutrition could only be acquired from microbiota or diet. It is used for modification of transfer RNA to protein transitional fidelity, but the specific microbial pathways evolved and the relationship with IBD are unclear. What this study addsThis study identifies a novel functional dysbiosis in IBD patients characterized by the depletion of q-producing gut bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes) and the downregulated microbial Q biosynthesis pathways, which correlates with host QTRT1 deficiency to potentially drive IBD pathogenesis. How this study might affect research, practice or policyO_LI1. Identifies the altered Q-biosynthesis pathway in human IBD. Establishes the "Microbial Q-synthesis-Host tRNA modification" axis as a novel mechanistic link, shifting human IBD microbiome research from taxonomic description to functional epitranscriptomics. C_LIO_LIOvercomes the inherent biases of traditional meta-analyses through a unified secondary bioinformatic reanalysis, leveraging HMP unified metabolic analysis network 3 (HUMAnN3)-based modeling of 3,000+ samples, to reveal a universal breakdown of the microbial Q-biosynthetic supply chain across all IBD subtypes. C_LIO_LIRecognize vitamin q as a critical gut-health micronutrient, influencing dietary guidelines and the regulation of functional medical foods for IBD management. C_LI

papers.title: METABOLIC DYSFUNCTION-ASSOCIATED STEATOTIC LIVER DISEASE IN PATIENTS WITH INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE: ASSOCIATION WITH BODY MASS INDEX AND DISEASE SEVERITY
papers.abstract: Whether body mass index (BMI) can meaningfully distinguish inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients with concomitant metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) was examined in a retrospective hospital series. The analysis covered 400 records from 2023-2024 with verified ulcerative colitis or Crohns disease and sufficient information on anthropometry, liver status, and intestinal disease activity. Normal BMI was documented in 118 patients, 176 were overweight, and 106 had obesity. MASLD classification required documented hepatic steatosis in the appropriate cardiometabolic setting; ultrasonography provided the principal evidence of steatosis, while laboratory findings, non-invasive indices, and elastography were considered when available. Ulcerative colitis activity was based on the Mayo Score and Crohns disease activity on CDAI. Overall, 181 patients (45.3%) met MASLD criteria. The corresponding frequencies across the three BMI strata were 20.3%, 49.4%, and 66.0% ({chi}2=49.29; p<0.001). Severe IBD was recorded in 6.8%, 14.8%, and 32.1%, respectively ({chi}2=39.45; p<0.001). Relative to normal BMI, the unadjusted odds of MASLD were 3.83-fold higher with overweight (95% CI 2.24-6.55) and 7.62-fold higher with obesity (95% CI 4.17-13.91). Thus, BMI categories identified groups with distinctly different burdens of both MASLD and severe IBD. Because treatment exposure, disease duration, and other covariates were not included in an adjusted model, the observed differences should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMSInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin, and diagnostic delay is associated with complications. We tested whether longitudinal machine learning using electronic health record (EHR) data can identify incident IBD before diagnosis, and quantified lead time and deployment burden. METHODSWe studied adults with an IBD-compatible symptom, sign, or finding at UCSF (2012-2024). Incident cases were confirmed by structured filtering and validated large language model note review. We trained a state space model (Mamba) and comparators on pre-diagnostic EHR data, excluding diagnostic-workup features, and assessed discrimination at 6- and 12-month landmarks. We externally tested Mamba without recalibration at ZSFG, a safety-net hospital serving a demographically and socioeconomically distinct population, and simulated diagnosis-code-only deployment at UCSF. RESULTSSix months after presentation, among patients still undiagnosed (67% of UCSF test cases), Mamba achieved an AUROC of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.928-0.999) at UCSF and 0.965 (0.952-0.976) at ZSFG. Median lead time was 20 months at UCSF and 15 months at ZSFG. Among future cases with an initially normal colonoscopy (N=32) or a histological finding of acute inflammation without chronicity (N=63), the model flagged 84% and 89% of these patients, respectively, before those procedures, indicating the potential for pre-diagnostic detection. Among 358,886 symptomatic patients not used for training (60 incident cases), the diagnosis-code-only model achieved an AUROC of 0.926; reviewing 20 alerts/month identified 34 cases (PPV, 1.09%; 64-fold above baseline). CONCLUSIONSLongitudinal machine learning can identify increased IBD risk months to years before diagnosis and may define a population for prospective studies of early IBD biology. Prospective evaluation should determine whether earlier identification reduces diagnostic delay. What You Need to KnowO_ST_ABSBackground and ContextC_ST_ABSIBD is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin. Whether routinely collected electronic health record data can identify future IBD before diagnosis, and at what alert burden, is unknown. New FindingsA longitudinal model identified future IBD six months after first symptomatic presentation with an AUROC of 0.97 and a median lead time of 20 months, with similar external discrimination. LimitationsThis was a retrospective study; external case labels were inferred rather than adjudicated, and colonoscopy analyses were exploratory. Whether earlier flagging shortens time to diagnosis requires prospective evaluation. Clinical Research RelevanceRoutinely collected structured EHR data could support targeted gastroenterology review of recurrently symptomatic patients. Because incident IBD is rare among symptomatic patients, a service reviewing 20 flagged charts per month would identify roughly one future case every five months. Deployment should therefore begin in silent mode, with locally calibrated thresholds and prospective measurement of alert burden. Basic Research RelevanceThe model flagged most future cases before a pre-diagnostic colonoscopy read as normal, or before biopsies showing only acute inflammation. Patients flagged despite normal-appearing mucosa may represent a preclinical population in which the earliest immunologic, serologic, and microbial events of IBD could be studied prospectively, including through model-guided mucosal sampling. Lay SummaryAn AI system reviewing medical records data is able to identify people who would later be diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease, often more than a year before doctors made the diagnosis.

papers.title: Longitudinal multi-omics profiling of tofacitinib response identifies a pre-existing Janus kinase-tractable inflammatory state in ulcerative colitis
papers.abstract: BO_SCPLOWACKGROUNDC_SCPLOWO_SCPCAP C_SCPCAP& OO_SCPLOWBJECTIVEC_SCPLOWTofacitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, is approved for ulcerative colitis (UC). We investigated baseline and longitudinal transcriptomics and proteomics in intestinal biopsies, peripheral blood, and serum from UC patients starting tofacitinib to characterize treatment-associated effects and identify which molecular compartment harbors the most predictive response-associated biomarkers. MO_SCPLOWETHODSC_SCPLOWIn this prospective, open-label study, patients with moderately to severely active UC started tofacitinib 10 mg BID for eight weeks. Clinical, biochemical, endoscopic, and histological data were collected at baseline and week 8. The primary outcome, histo-endoscopic mucosal improvement (HEMI), was defined as endoscopic Mayo subscore [≤]1 with histologic remission (Robarts Histopathology Index [≤]3, no mucosal neutrophils). Mucosal biopsies and peripheral blood were collected at baseline and week 8 for bulk RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq); biopsies and serum underwent proteomic profiling using Olink Explore 384 (Cardiometabolic, Inflammation, Neurology, Oncology panels). RO_SCPLOWESULTSC_SCPLOWIn total, 127 paired multi-omic samples were collected longitudinally from 40 UC patients: 15 (38%) achieved HEMI at week 8 (responders), 13 (32.5%) were late responders, and 12 (30%) were non-responders. Pretreatment mucosal biopsies from future responders showed elevated interferon, IL-6-family, IL-2/common-{gamma}-chain, and T-cell-receptor signaling gene expression, which declined on treatment only in responders. A responder-specific JAK-STAT-dependent mechanism spanned interferon, cytokine-receptor, T-cell-receptor, and NF-{kappa}B signaling, with concordant gene- and protein-level reductions. Compared with a public infliximab dataset, JAK-STAT/interferon downregulation was shared and response-independent, while non-canonical NF-{kappa}B downregulation was tofacitinib-specific. In blood, shared pathway labels reflected distinct genes from mucosal effectors. CO_SCPLOWONCLUSIONC_SCPLOWResponse to tofacitinib depends on a JAK-tractable mucosal pathway absent in non-responders, suggesting a pretreatment biomarker for predicting treatment response. What is already known on this topicPrior studies have individually interrogated transcriptomic and/or epigenomic signatures of tofacitinib response as a single modality. What this study addsOur study provides simultaneous profiling of both the transcriptome and proteome across paired mucosal and systemic compartments in patients, comparing responders with non-responders at baseline and over time. Our data support a model where tofacitinib response in UC depends on a JAK-dependent pro-inflammatory phenotype that the drug can dismantle, in contrast to non-responders representing distinct, JAK-independent pathways. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis study provides a foundation for treatment response studies in UC towards the development and validation of predictive biomarkers in colonic mucosa and blood, which could ultimately result in more personalized treatment strategies.

papers.title: Machine learning predicts relapse after anti-TNF withdrawal in ulcerative colitis using rectal biopsy transcriptomics
papers.abstract: BackgroundThere are currently no available biomarkers that predict the clinical outcome of ulcerative colitis (UC) patients after anti-TNF withdrawal. Here we developed a semi-supervised machine learning framework on RNA-seq data derived from rectal biopsies to predict relapse following anti-TNF discontinuation. MethodsWe included UC patients (n=136) enrolled in the prospective, randomized controlled BIOSTOP trial. Patients were assigned to a withdrawal group (stopped treatment immediately) or a maintenance group (stopped treatment after 2 years). A machine learning framework was trained on gene expression data from mucosal biopsies collected at baseline from the withdrawal group and validated in the maintenance group using baseline samples (test cohort) and 2-year follow-up samples (interference cohort). ResultsA semi-supervised machine learning model, combining a shared UMAP manifold representation with LabelSpreading on a targeted 38-gene panel achieved an AUC of 0.794, a sensitivity of 90.3%, and a specificity of 73.1% on the test cohort, and an AUC of 0.711, a sensitivity of 82.9%, and a specificity of 42.3% on the inference cohort. Applying Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) we found that IL1B, TYROBP, REG1B, S100A8, and TNF showed the highest predictive importance for relapse risk, whereas MUC2, HMGCS2, and CDKN1A displayed the highest predictive importance for sustained remission. ConclusionThe high sensitivity makes the model a promising screening tool to prevent withdrawal-related relapse, though its moderate specificity underscores the need for multi-center validation in larger, more diverse cohorts before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Integrated single-cell and proteomic profiling of pancreatic neoplasia identifies tissue markers that outperform established diagnostic markers in distinguishing cancer from precursor lesions.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) arises within an extensively remodeled microenvironment, yet tissue markers that distinguish invasive carcinoma from precursor lesions remain limited. Integrating four single-cell RNA-sequencing atlases comprising 324,662 cells from 26 patients, we identified cancer-associated fibroblast expansion, accumulation of C1QA+ immunoregulatory macrophages, and depletion of a dendritic-cell compartment expressing plasmacytoid markers. Fibroblasts were enriched for extracellular-matrix and PI3K-AKT programs and macrophages for an antigen-presentation program. We then examined the protein-level correlates of these populations in a tissue proteomic reference framework of 356 samples spanning non-diseased pancreas, normal-adjacent tissue, low- and high-grade intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma, and PDAC, prioritizing proteins that changed monotonically across the six histopathologic reference groups or marked tumor-enriched cell types. Despite depletion of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the principal source of type I interferon, the interferon-stimulated protein ISG15, expressed by both fibroblasts and macrophages, increased monotonically toward PDAC. In exploratory cross-validated benchmarking of PDAC versus low- and high-grade IPMN, excluding IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma (145 versus 56 samples), CATB+EPIPL achieved an AUC of 0.98, with a sensitivity of 92% at an achieved specificity of 92%, exceeding protein-abundance models of diagnostic IHC-associated markers (S100P+IMP3+maspin+MSLN, 0.79) and refitted published IPMN-progression combinations ([≤]0.91). Against non-diseased pancreas, candidate and comparator panels performed similarly (AUC 0.99-1.00). These biologically informed tissue protein panels warrant independent validation, including immunohistochemical evaluation of EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy specimens and measurement in blood.

papers.title: Change in irritable bowel syndrome symptom severity among members of a multi-omic digital food-as-medicine program: a retrospective single-arm cohort study with estimates corrected for regression to the mean
papers.abstract: BackgroundReal-world evidence on food-as-medicine programs for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is scarce, and single-arm evaluations overstate improvement because of regression to the mean (RTM). We estimated change in the IBS Symptom Severity Scale (IBS-SSS, 0-500) in a multi-omics personalized digital health food-as-medicine program, unadjusted and RTM-corrected. MethodsRetrospective single-arm cohort. Of 15,933 members with a valid baseline, 2,254 had a follow-up reading and 1,683 one at least 14 days after baseline. Change at 4, 12 (primary) and 26 weeks was estimated by baseline severity stratum, unadjusted and RTM-corrected by analysis of covariance. A responder fell by at least 50 points (the minimal clinically important difference benchmark). Sensitivity analyses covered equity, inverse-probability weighting and tipping-point analyses for members without a reading in each landmark window, a negative-control stratum and medication. The association of weight loss and dietary nutrient density with symptom change was evaluated within and between members. ResultsAt 12 weeks (n = 430) IBS-SSS fell by 43.88 points unadjusted (95% confidence interval [CI] -52.44 to -35.32; p < 0.001) and by 47.73 RTM-corrected (-55.48 to -39.98; p < 0.001); 720 of 1,339 symptomatic members (53.8%; 95% CI 51.1 to 56.4) fell by at least 50 points. Larger improvement in more severe members persisted after RTM correction (severe stratum, n = 37: unadjusted -127.43, RTM-corrected -60.71, 95% CI -97.75 to -23.68, p = 0.001). A higher meal nutrient density was associated with lower IBS-SSS within a members own trajectory (p = 0.018) while weight change was not (p = 0.361). Improvement was similar across groups in spite of baseline differences by age and sex: RTM-corrected 12-week change did not differ by age (p = 0.458), body-mass index (p = 0.328), sex (p = 0.749), income (p = 0.486) or ethnicity (p = 0.170). Estimates were robust to weighting for members without a reading in the landmark window (RTM-corrected estimates moved by less than 2 points), and the change of those members would have had to be 39 to 73 points worse than observed before the mean change reached zero. Baseline medication use and starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist did not explain symptom changes. ConclusionsIBS-SSS fell significantly among program participants, with steeper improvement in the more severe group, even after RTM correction. The improvement was comparable across socioeconomic characteristics, age and sex and robust to the confounders and missing-data assumptions evaluated. These associations from a self-selected single-arm cohort warrant replication in independent studies.

papers.title: Comprehensive proteomic characterization of the esophageal String Test identifies a luminal protein signature associated with eosinophilic esophagitis.
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe esophageal String Test (EST) is emerging as a minimally invasive alternative for assessing disease activity in eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE), yet the molecular composition of its protein content remains unknown. ObjectiveTo comprehensively characterize the esophageal EST proteome, define an EoE-associated luminal protein signature, and evaluate its biological and clinical relevance. MethodsEST samples were obtained from patients with active EoE, healthy controls (C) and patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Label-free proteomic profiling was performed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Differential protein accumulation, principal component analysis (PCA), pathway annotation, comparison with published esophageal tissue and salivary proteomes, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses and correlations with clinical disease activity were performed. ResultsMore than 3,000 proteins were identified in esophageal EST samples. Global proteomic profiling clearly separated patients with EoE from both C and GERD, whereas only limited differences were observed between the latter two groups. This enabled the identification of an EoE-associated luminal protein signature comprising inflammatory, epithelial, and tissue remodeling proteins. Comparison with published proteomic datasets indicated that the EST samples a complex esophageal luminal protein microenvironment containing proteins represented in esophageal mucosa and saliva, together with inflammatory and extracellular components. Several individual proteins showed high discriminatory performance in this exploratory cohort for distinguishing EoE from non-EoE subjects, and multiple proteins correlated with eosinophil counts and endoscopic measures of disease activity. ConclusionsThis study demonstrates that the EST provides access to a complex esophageal luminal protein microenvironment and establishes a molecular framework for its minimally invasive characterization in EoE.

papers.title: Preprocedural CT-guided anatomical assessment shortens intubation time and improves patient and operator experience during unsedated colonoscopy: a randomised controlled trial
papers.abstract: MESSAGELooping is a major cause of difficult and painful insertion during unsedated colonoscopy, yet strategies are largely guided by trial and error; prolonged insertion may jeopardise completion, discourage future surveillance and is associated with lower adenoma detection. In this randomised trial of 141 patients, protocolised review of pre-existing abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) anticipated colonic anatomy and shortened caecal intubation time by 136 s, while reducing pain, discomfort and operator workload and increasing willingness to repeat colonoscopy. Effects were largest in N-loop and alpha-loop configurations, which accounted for 83% of patients. Routinely acquired CT could support anatomy-informed colonoscope insertion especially when anesthesia services are limited or sedation poses an elevated risk.

papers.title: Causal relationship between liver fat reduction and clinical outcomes in human genetic studies and randomized clinical trials of metabolic-dysfunction associated steatohepatitis
papers.abstract: Reliance on invasive liver biopsy endpoints is a major limiting factor in new therapeutic development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). While liver fat accumulation is considered a driver of early disease, liver fat reduction is not recognized as a surrogate endpoint by health authorities. Here, we conducted the largest-to-date genome-wide association study (GWAS) of liver fat in 79,642 people with magnetic resonance imaging and developed a polygenic score with liver fat-lowering alleles across 55 genomic loci. In a separate set of 714,886 individuals, a 30% relative liver fat reduction due to the polygenic score was associated with 39% lower odds of liver cirrhosis and 41% lower odds of hepatocellular carcinoma, consistent with a strong causal relationship between lifelong liver fat differences and advanced liver clinical outcomes. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 randomized controlled trials including a total of 3,502 MASH patients showed that treatment-induced liver fat reductions were associated with MASH resolution (meta-regression slope in % units of the outcome for each 1% relative reduction in liver fat from baseline, {beta} = -0.70%, p<0.001) and fibrosis improvement ({beta} = -0.24%, p<0.001). These findings demonstrate the profound etiologic impact of liver fat in MASH and provide compelling evidence for liver fat reductions as a reasonably likely surrogate endpoint for future clinical development.

papers.title: Estimating sensitivity from tandem colonoscopy meta-analyses
papers.abstract: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSTandem colonoscopy meta-analyses estimate adenoma miss rates, which have been used as a proxy for colonoscopy sensitivity. Doing so overstates sensitivity because it ignores lesions missed by both exams. MethodsWe introduce Bayesian and frequentist approaches to estimate white-light colonoscopy (WLC) sensitivity from tandem colonoscopy meta-analyses. Neither approach assumes that the second colonoscopy is perfect. We apply both approaches to reanalyze data from a recent tandem colonoscopy meta-analysis, overall and across ten subgroups. Sensitivity analyses assess how assumptions about the relative performance of enhanced colonoscopy versus WLC affect estimates. ResultsUnder our Baseline specification, overall WLC sensitivity estimated by the Bayesian model was 0.54 [0.41, 0.63] (posterior mean and 95% credible interval). Sensitivity rose with lesion size: 0.49 [0.35, 0.60] for 1-5 mm adenomas, 0.64 [0.43, 0.78] for 6-9 mm adenomas and 0.84 [0.70, 0.93] for lesions 10 mm or larger. The frequentist plausible range encompassed the Bayesian estimate. The model-implied miss rate (0.35 [0.30, 0.40]) matched the original meta-analysis estimate and was stable across prior specifications. Assuming enhanced colonoscopy was perfect overstated overall sensitivity by 0.12 [0.06, 0.20]. LimitationsTandem colonoscopy data identify the miss rate but not WLC sensitivity, so estimates depend on an external assumption about the relative performance of enhanced colonoscopy versus WLC. As a result, WLC sensitivity estimates varied with the prior specification, especially for small and flat adenomas. ConclusionsWLC sensitivity may be meaningfully lower than previously assumed in CRC screening cost-effectiveness analyses. Modelers should use colonoscopy sensitivity estimates that do not assume a second colonoscopy exam is perfect.

papers.title: Identification of Transcriptional Hippo Response Signature Connecting Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Colorectal Cancer Progression
papers.abstract: BackgroundInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been linked to a two- to eightfold increase in colorectal cancer (CRC) risk. However, particular genes that bridge intestinal dysbiosis and oncogenic transcriptional reprogramming remain unclear. The Hippo/YAP pathway is a major regulator of intestinal epithelial homeostasis whose effector YAP is hyperactivated in CRC, but its transcriptional engagement in IBD mucosa and its link to specific cancer-risk genes has not been thoroughly mapped. MethodsBulk RNA-seq data were integrated from two independent cohorts: GSE235236 (IBD colon mucosa; UC/CD vs. healthy controls; n = 56) and TCGA-COAD/READ (CRC tumors stratified by YAP activity; n = 592). Differential expression analysis was conducted separately within each cohort using Welchs t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. YAP transcriptional activity was estimated per sample as the mean row-wise Z-score of seven canonical YAP target genes, and TCGA tumors were stratified into Hippo-High (Q4) and Hippo-Low (Q1) groups. Genes showing consistent dysregulation across both cohorts were identified and ranked to define a Dysbiosis-Hippo Response (DHR) module, which was further organized into functional gene archetypes. ResultsIBD mucosa showed 2,848 significantly dysregulated genes (FDR < 0.05). Comparison with the CRC cohort identified 120 genes showing concordant dysregulation, forming the DHR module. These genes were significantly enriched in TNF-alpha signaling via NF-kB (adjusted p = 0.006), inflammatory response (adjusted p = 0.013), and Myogenesis (adjusted p = 0.013). DHR gene classification revealed three functional archetypes: (i) innate immune activation (SPI1, OSM, IL11, LILRA2, SLC11A1) reflecting convergent myeloid reprogramming; (ii) epithelial-mesenchymal transition (TWIST1, SNAI1, PRRX2, MMP9) priming invasive potential before malignancy; and (iii) tumor microenvironment immune regulation (TN-FRSF4, TNFRSF18, PDCD1, VASN, SPON2) shaping immune tolerance. Interestingly, the canonical YAP target genes (CTGF, CYR61, ANKRD1, AMOTL2, and FSTL1), sharply upregulated in Hippo-High CRC, were essentially unchanged in IBD mucosa. This signifies that the shared DHR programme operates through non-canonical YAP effectors. And yet, YAP target scores are positively correlated with DHR module expression across IBD samples (Spearman rho = 0.726, p = 2.5 x 10-10). ConclusionsOur findings define a three-archetype DHR module that links gut dysbiosis to YAP-driven oncogenesis at single-gene resolution. The programme shared between IBD and CRC is driven by innate immune activation, EMT priming, and remodeling of the immune microenvironment, not by the canonical CTGF/CYR61 YAP target axis, which appears only at the CRC stage. This gene-level framework provides tractable mechanistic targets for chemoprevention and biomarker development at the inflammation-to-cancer transition.

papers.title: Circadian syndrome and incident non-neoplastic digestive disease in middle-aged and older Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCircadian syndrome (CircS) comprises metabolic abnormalities, short sleep, and depressive symptoms, and is associated with cardiovascular, liver, and lung diseases and mortality; evidence on digestive disease is scarce. We assessed its association with incident non-neoplastic digestive disease in Chinese adults. MethodsIn this prospective analysis of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), we included 2011 baseline participants aged [≥]45 years free of digestive disease, with follow-up to 2018. CircS ([≥]4 of 7 components) was analysed as a continuous score and as a binary exposure. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusting for demographic factors, BMI, smoking, and alcohol use. We did dose-response, component, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses; hs-CRP mediation was explored. Findings907 (19{middle dot}0%) of 4 771 participants developed digestive disease over a median 84 months. Each additional CircS component raised the risk by 9{middle dot}1% (HR 1{middle dot}091, 95% CI 1{middle dot}041-1{middle dot}144, P<0{middle dot}001); CircS positivity (36{middle dot}1%) was associated with a 25{middle dot}7% higher risk (HR 1{middle dot}257, 1{middle dot}084-1{middle dot}456, P=0{middle dot}002). Risk rose approximately linearly to about 70% higher at 5-7 components. Short sleep (HR 1{middle dot}178, 1{middle dot}017-1{middle dot}365) and depressive symptoms (HR 1{middle dot}570, 1{middle dot}367-1{middle dot}803) were the only independently associated components; no metabolic component was associated. Results were robust across sensitivity analyses; hs-CRP did not mediate the association. InterpretationCircS is associated with incident non-neoplastic digestive disease, driven by its circadian-emotional rather than metabolic components. Sleep and mood may be targets for prevention. FundingThis research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

papers.title: Implementation of risk prediction models using electronic health data for early detection of pancreatic cancer: a prospective pilot feasibility study
papers.abstract: Background & AimsWe previously developed multiple machine-learning and regression-based risk prediction models using retrospective electronic health records (EHR) to estimate near-term risk of pancreatic cancer (PC). This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of an early detection strategy combining initial EHR-based risk prediction with downstream imaging and blood-based testing. MethodsThis prospective study included adults aged 50-84 years with an estimated [≥]1% 18-month risk of PC, identified between January 2021 and March 2023 using four previously validated models. Patients with a history or active suspicion of PC were excluded. Participants completed cross-sectional imaging and CA19-9 labs at baseline and again at 18 months. Outcomes included enrollment rates, test completion rate, and burden of incidental findings. ResultsOf 1,251 eligible patients, 102 (8.2%) enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 58% women; 48% Hispanic, 34% White, 11% Black, and 7% Asian). At baseline, 89 (87%) completed imaging and 98 (96%) completed CA19-9. At 18 months, 79% completed both imaging and CA19-9. Ten (10%) participants underwent additional clinical evaluations triggered by imaging findings. Evaluations included an endoscopic ultrasound, renal imaging, and FibroScan. CA19-9 results were normal in most participants, though 18% had elevated levels at baseline. ConclusionsReal-time EHR-based ML algorithms can be combined with blood- and imaging-based surveillance for early detection of PC with acceptable burden of incidental findings. However, improved patient engagement is a key aspect that will need to be addressed in order to successfully scale an AI-guided strategy for early detection.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Profiling and Demographic Analysis of Appalachian Patients with Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma using the Purity Independent Subtyping of Tumors (PurIST) Classifier
papers.abstract: PURPOSEPancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a deadly malignancy with poor prognosis. A transcriptomic-based algorithm called Purity Independent Subtyping of Tumors (PurIST) relies on expression profiling of a defined set of genes to stratify PDAC into classical and basal-like molecular subtypes and assigns a confidence level to the subtypes as either "strong," "likely," or "lean." In this study, we apply PurIST to Appalachian and non-Appalachian patient cohorts and assess demographic variables between groups that may influence treatment outcomes. PATIENTS AND METHODSThis 13-site study includes 780 PDAC patients. Patients were divided into Appalachian and non-Appalachian cohorts according to Appalachian Regional Commission guidelines, and differences in PurIST classification, tobacco use, and alcohol use were analyzed. RESULTSIndividuals from Appalachian regions were more likely to receive a subtype classification from PurIST with "strong" confidence as opposed to "likely" or "lean" (P=0.0175; odds ratio=1.66). We did not observe any significant difference between basal and classical subtype classification in Appalachia (P=0.1457), yet an exploratory analysis showed that individuals aged [≥]85 were significantly more likely to have basal-like tumor classifications (P=0.005817; odds ratio=3.79). Appalachian patients were more likely to have a history of smoking (59.6% vs 49.9%; P=0.01756) and less likely to report alcohol consumption (50.5% vs 65.6%; P=0.000229). CONCLUSIONWe conducted the largest comparison of the PurIST algorithm in Appalachia to date and found PurIST is more likely to have higher confidence in molecular subtype classifications for Appalachian PDAC tumors compared to non-Appalachian tumors. If PurIST is to be considered as a prognostic or decision-making tool for PDAC patients, we must account for variability in different populations and model the likelihood that tumors will have a strong molecular signature.

papers.title: Microbial guild architecture transduces multi-component botanical inputs into multi-receptor-mediated gut motility restoration
papers.abstract: How ecological architectures within the gut microbiome convert complex inputs into specific host physiological outcomes remains poorly understood. We used CDD-2101, a multi-component botanical drug operating under an FDA (U.S. Food and Drug Administration) Investigational New Drug program, as a defined ecological perturbation in functional constipation (FC). Integrating a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial with genome-resolved metagenomics, targeted metabolomics, staged prediction modeling, and receptor-level validation, we show that clinical efficacy of CDD-2101 depends on remodeling a function-specific substructure of the stable Two Competing Guilds (TCG) architecture. We term this substructure the FC-TCG, demonstrate its role along the gut-motility axis, and confirm its effect in three independent gut hypomotility cohorts. The two guilds responded asymmetrically: the intervention selectively suppressed the C1B guild (the pathobiont guild) while largely sparing the C1A guild, the foundation guild that anchors the core gut community, restoring its ecological dominance, producing a coordinated metabolic shift that elevates lithocholic acid and propionic acid. Through gnotobiotic transplantation and receptor antagonism, we demonstrate that lithocholic acid and propionic acid restore gut motility via concurrent engagement of Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5) and G-protein coupled receptor 43 (GPR43). These findings identify microbial guild architecture as a function-resolved signal-transducing layer that converts multi- component botanical intervention into multi-receptor-mediated gut motility restoration, reframing the gut microbiome from a compositional system into a structural transducer between complex environmental inputs and host physiology. HighlightsO_LIA gut motility-supporting Two-Competing-Guilds module (FC-TCG) was identified via a randomized clinical trial with quality-controlled botanical intervention as an ecological perturbation. C_LIO_LIGuild architecture translates multi-component botanical inputs into coordinated metabolite signals. C_LIO_LIGuild restructuring increases lithocholic acid and propionic acid to restore gut motility by activating TGR5 and GPR43. C_LIO_LIMicrobial guilds constitute a signal-transducing layer linking complex environmental inputs to host physiology. C_LI Significance StatementThis study establishes a mechanistic link between stable microbial guild architecture and host physiological control. By resolving the Two-Competing-Guilds (TCG) structure into a function-specific module, it demonstrates how complex environmental inputs restructure the ecological system into coordinated metabolites programs and receptor-level signaling. The findings show that, among the gut microbiome ecological system, microbial guilds act as a signal-transducing layer that converts botanical complexity into targeted host responses. This provides a generalizable system level strategy for dissecting microbiome-mediated mechanisms of multi-component interventions and advances a systems-level understanding of environment- microbiome-host interactions. papers.title: Predicting Early MASLD-HCC from Serum N-Glycomics: A SHAP-Interpreted Gaussian Naive Bayes Model Built on nLC-HCD-PRM-MS/MS Profiling
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) arising from Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) is an increasing public health burden with high mortality, highlighting the need for improved early detection strategies. Current surveillance tools, including Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and ultrasound, lack sufficient sensitivity for early-stage HCC detection. We analyzed serum samples from 131 patients, including 58 with cirrhosis and 73 with MASLD-related HCC (42 early-stage, 31 late-stage), using an nLC-stepped HCD-PRM-MS/MS workflow for targeted N-glycome profiling of glycopeptides derived from haptoglobin and vitronectin. Combining targeted glycopeptides with AFP significantly improved HCC detection compared with AFP alone. The optimal panel for all HCC versus cirrhosis (AFP + VTNC_169_A2G2F0S1 + VTNC_242_A3G3F2S2) achieved an AUC of 0.859 and 76.7% sensitivity at 90% specificity. For early-stage HCC, AFP + HP_184_A3G3F1S3 + VTNC_169_A2G2F0S1 yielded an AUC of 0.890 with 66.7% sensitivity at 1% specificity. A SHAP-selected Gaussian Naive Bayes model based on seven molecular/glycopeptide features, without demographic variables, further improved performance, achieving ROC-AUC values of 0.9985 in training and 1.0000 in independent testing cohorts, with accuracies of 98.1% and 100.0%, respectively. papers.title: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Fibrosis Score (MAF-5) and Gallstone Prevalence: A Cross-Sectional Analysis Using NHANES 2017-2020 Data
papers.abstract: BackgroundGallstones are one of the most common gastrointestinal conditions closely associated with metabolic dysfunction. The metabolic dysfunction-associated fibrosis-5 (MAF-5) score has been established as a non-invasive indicator for assessing liver fibrosis in individuals with metabolic abnormalities. However, comprehensive large-scale research examining the correlation between the MAF-5 score and gallstone occurrence remains limited. This study seeks to clarify the link between the MAF-5 score and gallstone prevalence using nationally representative data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). MethodsThis study examined data from 15,560 NHANES 2017-2020 participants aged 20 years or older, ensuring complete records for MAF-5 scores and gallstone status. Gallstone presence was identified through self-reported physician diagnoses. To assess the relationship between MAF-5 scores and gallstone prevalence, weighted logistic regression models were applied, adjusting for demographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, and health conditions. Subgroup analyses were conducted to evaluate the stability of this association and detect possible interactions. Sensitivity analyses were performed by excluding extreme values ({+/-}3SD) to assess result robustness. Furthermore, MAF-5 scores were divided into quartiles to investigate gallstone prevalence trends, and a restricted cubic spline (RCS) model was employed to visualize response patterns. ResultsA total of 15,560 participants met the inclusion criteria, with 747 in the gallstone group and 6,367 in the non-gallstone group. MAF-5 scores were significantly higher in the gallstone group (P < 0.001). After adjusting for multiple covariates, each unit increase in MAF-5 score correlated with a 14% higher gallstone prevalence (OR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.06-1.23). Quartile-based analysis indicated that individuals in the highest MAF-5 quartile had a 2.12-fold higher prevalence of gallstones than those in the lowest quartile (OR = 2.12, 95% CI: 1.13-3.98). RCS analysis confirmed a linear association between MAF-5 scores and gallstone prevalence. Subgroup analyses showed this association remained stable across age, sex, and racial/ethnic groups, with no significant interactions. Sensitivity analyses, excluding extreme values ({+/-}3SD), reinforced the reliability of these findings (OR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.04-1.28). ConclusionThe MAF-5 score is significantly and positively associated with gallstone prevalence, independent of demographic and lifestyle confounders. These findings indicate that the MAF-5 score may be a useful tool for assessing gallstone prevalence in individuals with metabolic dysfunction, offering valuable insights for early screening and targeted health management strategies.

papers.title: Itopride hydrochloride extended-release vs film-coated tablets for gastrointestinal symptoms in functional dyspepsia
papers.abstract: BackgroundFunctional dyspepsia (FD) is among the most common gastrointestinal disorders worldwide and is characterized by symptoms including epigastric pain, early satiety, postprandial fullness, bloating, and upper abdominal discomfort. Itopride hydrochloride is commonly administered as 50 mg three times daily (TID). To improve convenience and potentially enhance adherence, a once-daily (OD) 150 mg extended-release formulation was developed. Phase 1 studies demonstrated bioequivalent overall exposure between the OD and TID regimens, with sustained-release characteristics and no evidence of dose dumping, supporting advancement to Phase 3. This pivotal clinical study evaluated whether itopride hydrochloride 150 mg OD is non-inferior to the established 50 mg TID regimen in improving FD symptoms over 8 weeks. MethodsThis Phase 3, randomized, open-label, multicenter, active-controlled study enrolled 564 participants with FD (or chronic gastritis) to compare the efficacy and safety of itopride hydrochloride 150 mg OD versus 50 mg TID over 8 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in overall FD severity from baseline to Week 8, assessed using the Leeds Dyspepsia Questionnaire (LDQ) severity score. Secondary endpoints included symptom-specific severity, disease-specific quality of life, responder rates, treatment acceptance, and safety. ResultsClinical non-inferiority in terms of overall FD severity was demonstrated with OD treatment compared to TID. LDQ severity improved by -9.60 (95% CI -10.15, -9.05) with TID and -9.76 (95% CI -10.32, -9.19) with OD, with a between-group difference of 0.16 (95% CI -0.42, 0.74). Improvements across symptom domains and quality of life measures were comparable. Treatment acceptance favored OD (mean 4.22 vs 3.83; p < 0.001). Both regimens were well tolerated, with predominantly mild adverse events. This clinical evaluation of OD was supported by the Phase 1 results confirming that both single-dose and multiple-dose administration of itopride hydrochloride 150 mg OD provided a comparable extent of exposure to the 50 mg TID regimen, demonstrated by area under the curve (AUC) values within the 80-125% bioequivalence range and stable pharmacokinetic profiles across fed and fasted conditions. ConclusionThe study confirmed that itopride hydrochloride 150 mg OD is non-inferior to the TID regimen for improving FD (or chronic gastritis) symptoms. The OD regimen demonstrated comparable efficacy, favorable treatment acceptance, and a positive benefit-risk profile, offering a more convenient therapeutic option for patients.
